content: The release and retention of active ingredients in a product must be carefully controlled to avoid releasing the ingredient too quickly or too slowly. While no test can fully replicate all real-world conditions, the testing methods used aim to provide a general indication of whether the release and retention are acceptable when the product is used as directed on its label. This is particularly relevant for slow-release capsule suspensions, granules, and multi-character liquid formulations. Testing methods for this are product-specific, and appropriate methods must be available. General limits cannot be universally defined, as the free active ingredient may exist in solution, emulsion, or on the outer surface of capsule walls. By-products from manufacturing or storage, such as impurities, must be limited to reduce risks associated with handling or using the product and to maintain the formulation's efficacy. This applies to all specifications where relevant impurities may be associated with the active ingredient. Analytical methods for detecting these impurities must be peer-validated and submitted to the appropriate authorities (e.g., FAO or WHO) for evaluation if not already published. The maximum permitted impurity levels should be expressed as grams per kilogram of the active ingredient. In exceptional cases, where impurities in a formulation component can increase the content of a relevant impurity, the maximum content may be specified on a formulation basis rather than the active ingredient basis. Water content in technical materials, concentrates, and non-aqueous formulations must be limited to prevent adverse effects on storage stability or the quality of subsequent formulations. The Karl Fischer method, using pyridine-free reagents, is the preferred testing method. Water is considered a relevant impurity if it could affect water-sensitive formulations or if it is not adequately controlled by other clauses. Insoluble materials in technical materials and concentrates must also be limited to prevent issues such as filter or nozzle blockages during field use. Testing methods include ethanol, sodium hydroxide, water, xylene, acetone, and oil insolubility tests. The maximum permitted level must be stated in grams per kilogram of the active ingredient. Physical properties of formulations are grouped into categories such as density, surface properties, volatility, particulate properties, dispersion, flow, and solution properties. These tests provide models to assess performance under controlled conditions, though they cannot fully predict field performance. Limits for satisfactory performance are based on experience and are indicative rather than definitive. For example, suspension tests require at least 60% of the active ingredient to remain in suspension. For example, granules must flow freely from application machinery and resist attrition to minimize dust generation. Similarly, tablets must remain intact during handling and application, with no broken tablets allowed in a package. For example, at least 60% of the active ingredient must remain in dispersion for suspension concentrates and capsule suspensions. Limits are product-dependent and must be validated. Acidity, alkalinity, or pH range must be controlled to prevent decomposition of the active ingredient, deterioration of physical properties, or container corrosion. These parameters are expressed as grams per kilogram of sulfuric acid or sodium hydroxide, depending on the nature of the formulation.
